text: I burned the first tray of baklava on a Thursday that already smelled like bleach. My uncle swore in two languages, then handed me a cracked plastic scraper like that was the whole curriculum. The third tray I over-honeyed until the pan dripped on my shoe. What I actually kept from that year was a way of standing: hips angled toward the oven, one ear on the dining room, counting the walk-in fridge's bad compressor. I still listen for machines that are about to fail.

text: Repairing an old motorcycle was an unexpected classroom. I began with little knowledge, but I was determined to understand how the system worked. text: The branch library on Fourth smells like warm dust and copier toner. I shelved there for two summers. Kids left stickers inside the picture books, which is a form of criticism I respect. A regular named Dot asked me every Wednesday if we had 'the new James,' meaning Patterson, and I learned to say not yet without making it a moral failure. I started reading the things people returned with receipts still in them. Bus transfers. A court date. A recipe in another handwriting. I did not take the receipts. I just noticed that a library is a machine for almost-privacy. When I write now, I leave a little room in the margin. Not because it is poetic. Because people need somewhere to put a sticker.
